title: The Legend of Suriyothai
full_review:
The fabled tale of Queen Suriyothai, a heroine of medieval Siam who died valiantly in battle against Burmese aggressors, is brought to life in the lavish historical epic "The Legend of Suriyothai" (Sony Classics).

Directed by Chatrichalerm Yukol -- a bona fide Thai prince himself -- and billed as the most expensive Thai movie ever produced, the visually sumptuous spectacle is weighed down by a cumbersome plot, obfuscated by a myriad of characters whose exotic, tongue-twister names change with rank, making scorekeeping a royal headache.

Based on years of research and drawing from historical first-person accounts of Portuguese travelers, the labyrinthine narrative chronicles the incessant power grabs by rival factions vying for the crown of what is now Thailand. Siam of the 16th century was a confederacy of small kingdoms united under a two-pronged throne consisting of the realm of Ayothaya in the South, seat of the semi-divinized "King of Kings," and Pitsanulok in the North, ruled by a lesser monarch known as the "Second King" -- with neighboring Burma, the "great enemy," casting a constant pall of war over their sovereignty.

Audiences are first introduced to the eponymous Siamese queen (M.L. Piyapas Bhirombhakdi) while still a young princess. She is bored with court life and longs to break free of the stifling shackles imposed by protocol -- like any modern teen, she wants to do her "own thing." Having revealed that she has never even stepped foot outside the royal palace, it comes as no surprise that when she is allowed to attend a royal elephant roundup -- chaperoned by a small army of ladies-in-waiting -- and the opportunity for a brief escape presents itself, she pounces on it.

Giving her entourage the slip, she enjoys a few moments alone with, what else, a boy -- her distant cousin, the dashing Lord Piren (Chatchai Plengpanich), a gallant warrior. After they vow mutual eternal love, Piren swears by his knightly honor to remain forever in her service. The fairy-tale interlude quickly ends.
Suriyothai is soon given in marriage to Prince Tienraja (Sarunyu Wongkrachang), son of the Second King. Distraught, she runs away, but is caught and brought before the "King of Kings," who is conveniently encamped nearby. His majesty offers to annul the agreement, but warns her that doing so would create a dangerous rift between the North and South kingdoms. Faced with choosing between love and duty, Suriyothai obliges obediently, marking the first sacrifice she will make for her country.

The remainder of the nearly two and a half hours is a bloody, at times tedious, cataloguing of internecine court intrigues, assassinations and coups plotted by the loosely aligned nobles jockeying for power, who employ such grisly machinations as poisonings and ritual beheadings in their pursuit of all the dynastic marbles. (Yukol's friend and fellow UCLA alum Francis Ford Coppola, no slouch at "whacking" the competition, served as the film's executive producer.)

Surprisingly, for long stretches Suriyothai is banished to the periphery, watching much of the action unfold from the narrative sidelines and re-emerging toward the climax, as invading Burmese forces threaten the survival of Siam. Appearing somewhat out of left field, she mounts her painted war elephant and rides off to battle, absorbing a mortal blow intended for her royal husband. Many of the meaty scenes are stolen by the Machiavellian concubine Srisudachan (Mai Charoenpura), the most deliciously evil social climber since Lady Macbeth.

While boasting visual bravura -- including money shots of imperial splendor and massive battlefield sequences -- the narrative suffers from an overabundance of characters and a choppy story line, with pivotal action occurring off-screen -- a consequence of the lengthy film being trimmed down from its unmanageable original running time of more than four hours. Contrasting the ornate saffron and gold set-pieces are the rather monotone performances of the leads -- more likely attributable to the Eastern culture's tradition of emotional reserve than to bad acting.

In Shakespearean fashion, the film serves chivalrous virtue and venomous revenge in equal measure. Nevertheless, viewers may justifiably find the graphic carnage more than a bit off-putting, especially the scenes depicting brutal executions, two of which include the murder of young children.

Subtitles.

Due to recurring gory violence on and off the battlefield as well as fleeting nudity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
